title: Adani Ports buys Europe's fuel tanks in a Rs 27,142 crore deal
subtitle: India's biggest private port operator will own 452 storage tanks at eight European ports, its first liquid storage outside India.
content_html:
Picture a steel tank taller than a house, filled with fuel, standing at a port in Rotterdam. Then picture 452 of them, spread over eight ports in Europe. On Thursday, 5 November 2026, India's Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) announced a plan to buy the company that runs all of them: a Dutch company named Evos.

The full price tag is 2.56 billion euros, or Rs 27,142 crore. Mint reports this will be the largest deal Adani Ports has ever done, and the first time the company will own liquid storage tanks outside India.

What does Evos actually do?

Think of Evos as a giant parking lot, but for liquids instead of cars. Ships arrive with petrol, diesel, jet fuel or ship fuel. The liquid goes into big tanks and waits. Later it leaves on another ship, on a barge (a flat river boat), or through a pipeline.

Evos is Europe's second-largest independent liquid storage operator. It earns by renting tank space to others, the way a cold storage owner rents space to many farmers. Its customers include big energy companies, chemical makers and commodity traders, according to the company filing reported by Business Standard.

Here is Evos in numbers, from that same filing:

  • 8 terminals at ports: Amsterdam East, Amsterdam West, Rotterdam and Terneuzen in the Netherlands, Ghent in Belgium, Hamburg in Germany, Algeciras in Spain, and one in Malta.
  • 452 tanks, with space for 6.3 million cubic metres of liquid.
  • 63 berths, the parking spots where ships and barges tie up.
  • Pipeline links, including one to Schiphol airport.
  • 37 million tonnes of liquid handled in 2025.

How big is 6.3 million cubic metres? One cubic metre holds 1,000 litres. So Evos can hold about 630 crore litres. Adani Ports has 5.5 million cubic metres across five Indian ports. That means Evos alone has more tank space than all of Adani Ports' tanks in India put together.

Why would a port company want fuel tanks?

A port works like a railway station for goods. Boxes travel in containers. But oil, chemicals and fuels travel as liquids, and they need tanks to wait in before the next trip. Evos also stores newer fuels like sustainable aviation fuel, biofuels, methanol and bioethanol, the filing says.

A big part of the rent comes from take-or-pay contracts. The idea is simple: a customer books tank space and pays for it even if the tank sits half empty, like paying the monthly fee for a locker you forgot to use. On average, 99 per cent of Evos's tank space is booked, Business Today reports.

That is why Evos makes steady money. In 2025 it earned revenue of 392 million euros and EBITDA of 219 million euros. EBITDA is the money left from running the business before paying interest, tax and the wear and tear on machines. Think of a samosa stall: the day's sales minus flour, oil and the cook's pay, before the shop loan EMI. Evos keeps 56 per cent of its sales as EBITDA. Adani Ports' own foreign ports kept 44.8 per cent in April to September 2026, the same report says.

Karan Adani, managing director of Adani Ports, said in the company's statement:

"We look forward to partnering with Europe, supporting its sustainable energy transition and creating enduring value while maintaining the financial prudence that underpins our growth."

Enterprise value, in simple words

Two numbers float around in this deal, and they look very different. Adani Ports will pay 1.18 billion euros (Rs 12,511 crore) for all of Evos's shares. But the headline number is 2.56 billion euros. Why the gap?

Imagine buying a friend's cycle shop for Rs 50,000. The shop also has a Rs 60,000 bank loan, and now you must repay it. The real cost to you is Rs 1,10,000. That full amount, the price of the shares plus the debt you take over, is called the enterprise value.

Same here. Adani Ports pays 1.18 billion euros in cash and also takes on Evos's debt, which brings the total to 2.56 billion euros. So the debt part is about 1.38 billion euros.

Where does the money come from?

Adani Ports will pay with borrowed money. The deal still needs approval from regulators and talks with works councils, which are groups that speak for workers inside European companies. Mint reports Adani Ports will buy the full stake over the coming 15 months.

A common way to check whether a loan is too heavy is to compare it with yearly EBITDA. For Adani Ports and Evos together, net debt comes to 2.76 times a year's EBITDA, and the company expects this to fall to about 2.5 times by FY27. In plain words, the total loans equal a little under three years of operating earnings. Adani Ports also had Rs 12,502 crore of cash at the end of September 2026, the Tribune report adds.

Adani Ports' world map keeps growing

Adani Ports began on 26 May 1998 as Mundra Port and Special Economic Zone Limited, in Gujarat. Today it is India's largest private port operator, says Wikipedia.

Evos will be its fifth foreign buy in five years. It already runs terminals in Israel, Tanzania, Sri Lanka and Australia. Chief executive Ashwani Gupta told analysts on Thursday evening that the company was weighing 20 buying chances around the world, Mint reports. Once Evos joins, the network will reach 28 ports and terminals across 10 countries.

What the deal changes

For Adani Ports, Evos brings earnings in euros. The company says Evos adds "predictable hard-currency cash flows", meaning money that comes in a strong foreign currency, not in rupees.

For trade, an Indian company will now sit in the middle of Europe's fuel flow. Evos's tanks are linked by pipeline to Schiphol airport. Once the deal closes, an Indian company will own the tanks at one end of that pipe.
